blocks.text: 1. One-Class SVM

blocks.alt: Normal data only learns a boundary that separates inside from outside

blocks.text: Isolation Forest, the previous topic, measures anomalousness indirectly, through how quickly a point gets isolated by random tree splits. One-Class SVM takes yet another distinct approach, adapting the maximum margin idea already covered in depth for Support Vector Machine in the Classification module. Rather than measuring isolation difficulty, it explicitly learns a single, well-defined geometric boundary that wraps as tightly as reasonably possible around the region of feature space containing normal, typical data.

Once this boundary has been learned from the training data, any new point that falls inside it is classified as normal, and any new point that falls outside it is flagged as a potential anomaly. This gives One-Class SVM a genuinely different character from Isolation Forest: rather than an implicit, score-based signal built from many random trees, it produces one explicit, geometrically interpretable decision boundary, directly extending the same margin-based reasoning already built up for ordinary, two-class SVM.
2. Adapting SVM to a Single Class

blocks.alt: Standard SVM separates two classes while one-class SVM works with one class only

blocks.text: Ordinary Support Vector Machine, covered in depth in the Classification module, finds the maximum margin boundary that best separates two known, labeled classes from each other, using labeled training examples of both classes to determine exactly where that boundary should sit. One-Class SVM faces a fundamentally different situation: only one class exists in the training data, examples of normal behavior, with no labeled anomaly examples available to separate it from at all.

This is precisely the scenario the name one-class refers to, and it required a genuine adaptation of the underlying SVM machinery, since the original two-class margin-maximization objective has no direct meaning when there is only a single class of labeled data to work with. One-Class SVM's specific adaptation, covered in the next section, reuses the same maximum-margin and kernel-trick machinery already built for ordinary SVM, just repurposed to answer this fundamentally different, single-class question.
3. Why Training on Normal Data Alone Matters

The situation One-Class SVM is built for, having only normal examples available for training with no labeled anomalies at all, is not a contrived edge case; it is exactly the situation Anomaly Detection usually faces in real practice. Genuine anomalies, whether fraudulent transactions, failing equipment, or novel security intrusions, are by definition rare, and in many real settings the specific kinds of anomalies that will occur in the future have simply never been observed at all in the historical training data.

This makes training a normal two-class classifier, which would need labeled examples of both normal and anomalous behavior, often impractical or outright impossible in genuine anomaly detection settings. One-Class SVM is purpose-built specifically to work in exactly this constrained situation, learning what normal looks like purely from examples of normal behavior, without ever needing a single labeled anomaly example during training at all.
4. The Origin Trick

blocks.alt: Normal points get separated from the origin

blocks.text: One-Class SVM's specific mathematical adaptation is often explained through what is sometimes called the origin trick. Rather than separating two classes of real data from each other, the algorithm treats the coordinate origin, or more precisely a synthetic representation of the absence of data, as a stand-in for the anomaly class, and then finds the maximum margin hyperplane that best separates all of the actual normal training data from that origin.

Equivalently, and perhaps more intuitively, this can be understood as finding the smallest possible region in feature space that still contains almost all of the normal training data, while excluding as much of the surrounding empty space as possible. Once this region has been learned, any new point falling inside it is classified as normal, and any new point falling outside it, in the excluded surrounding space, is flagged as a potential anomaly, exactly the decision rule One-Class SVM applies at prediction time.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The origin trick is a mathematical device for adapting SVM's two-class margin machinery to a single-class problem; the practical, intuitive result is simply a learned boundary that wraps around wherever normal data actually sits in feature space.

blocks.text: 5. The Kernel Trick, Reapplied

Real normal data very rarely forms a simple, cleanly linearly separable region in raw feature space; it is much more common for the region containing normal behavior to have a genuinely curved, irregular shape. One-Class SVM addresses this exactly the same way ordinary SVM addressed the analogous problem back in the Classification module: through the kernel trick, most commonly using the RBF kernel already covered there in depth.

The RBF kernel implicitly maps the data into a higher-dimensional space where a clean, linear boundary around the normal data becomes achievable, without ever needing to explicitly compute that higher-dimensional mapping directly, exactly the computational efficiency the kernel trick was built to provide. Mapped back down into the original feature space, this learned boundary can take on an arbitrarily curved, flexible shape, letting One-Class SVM wrap tightly around genuinely irregular regions of normal behavior that a simple linear or purely statistical boundary could never capture accurately.
6. The nu Parameter

blocks.alt: A low nu expects few outliers while a high nu expects many outliers

blocks.text: One-Class SVM's key hyperparameter is called nu, which roughly represents the expected fraction of training points that will be allowed to fall outside the learned boundary, and simultaneously serves as an upper bound on the fraction of anomalies expected in the training data itself. Setting nu to a small value, such as 0.01, draws the boundary tightly, allowing only a very small fraction of the normal training points to fall outside it, which correspondingly leads to fewer points being flagged as anomalies at prediction time on new data.

Setting nu to a larger value, such as 0.2, draws the boundary more loosely, deliberately allowing a larger fraction of the training points to fall outside it, which correspondingly leads to more points being flagged as anomalies at prediction time. Choosing nu well requires some genuine understanding, or at least a reasonable estimate, of how much noise or how many mild outliers already exist within what is being treated as the normal training data itself.

blocks.text: 7. One-Class SVM versus Isolation Forest

blocks.alt: One-Class SVM is boundary based while Isolation Forest is isolation based

blocks.text: One-Class SVM and Isolation Forest, the two topics covered so far in this module beyond the Z-Score Method, take genuinely different structural approaches to the same underlying problem. Isolation Forest produces no explicit boundary at all; it works entirely through an implicit, score-based signal built from averaging isolation difficulty across many random trees, and it scales efficiently to large datasets with relatively little parameter tuning required beyond the handful of hyperparameters already covered.

One-Class SVM instead produces one explicit, well-defined geometric boundary, and through the kernel trick it can capture more precise, intricately shaped boundaries around genuinely complex, curved regions of normal behavior. This precision, however, comes at a real computational cost: kernel-based SVM methods generally scale less favorably to very large datasets than Isolation Forest's random-tree approach does, making the choice between the two often come down directly to dataset size and how much boundary precision genuinely matters for the problem at hand.

blocks.text: 8. Feature Scaling Still Matters

blocks.alt: Unscaled features make one-class SVM unreliable

blocks.text: Because One-Class SVM is built directly on the same margin and kernel machinery already covered for ordinary Support Vector Machine, it inherits exactly the same sensitivity to feature scale already established in that earlier topic. The margin and kernel calculations both depend on distances or dot products between points in feature space, and if one feature spans a much larger numeric range than another, that large-range feature will dominate the learned boundary almost entirely, exactly the same problem already covered for ordinary SVM.

Standardizing every feature to zero mean and unit variance before fitting a One-Class SVM, using the same Feature Scaling module techniques applied consistently throughout this course, remains essential here for exactly the same reasons it was essential for ordinary SVM. Skipping this step can produce a learned boundary that reflects arbitrary differences in measurement units far more than any genuine structure in what actually constitutes normal behavior.
9. When One-Class SVM Fits Well

blocks.alt: A clear normal region points toward one-class SVM being a good fit

blocks.text: One-Class SVM is particularly well suited to situations where only normal examples are genuinely available for training, with no labeled anomalies at all, exactly the realistic scenario common across fraud detection, network intrusion detection, and manufacturing defect detection, where the specific anomalies that will eventually occur are often entirely unseen at training time. It is also a strong choice whenever the region of normal behavior is expected to have a genuinely complex, non-convex shape that a simpler statistical threshold, like the Z-Score Method's Normal-distribution assumption, could not adequately capture.

On moderately sized datasets, One-Class SVM's computational cost remains entirely manageable, and its kernel-based flexibility often pays off directly in more accurate boundary shapes. On very large datasets, its comparatively higher computational cost relative to Isolation Forest becomes a more serious practical consideration, and Isolation Forest, or one of the density-based methods covered in the remaining topics of this module, may become the more practical choice.
10. Worked Example
The example below fits a One-Class SVM on normal training data alone and evaluates it on a mix of normal and clearly anomalous test points.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

# Training data: only normal points, no labeled anomalies at all
normal_training_data = rng.normal(loc=[50, 50], scale=5, size=(200, 2))

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(normal_training_data)

model = OneClassSVM(kernel='rbf', nu=0.05, gamma='scale')
model.fit(X_train_scaled)

# Test data: a mix of normal points and a few clear anomalies
test_points = np.array([
    [51, 49], [48, 52], [50, 50],   # should look normal
    [10, 10], [90, 90], [5, 95],    # should look anomalous
])
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(test_points)

predictions = model.predict(X_test_scaled)  # 1 for normal, -1 for anomaly
scores = model.decision_function(X_test_scaled)  # positive means inside the boundary

for point, pred, score in zip(test_points, predictions, scores):
    label = "normal" if pred == 1 else "ANOMALY"
    print(f"Point {point}: {label} (score={score:.3f})")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: decision_function returns a positive value for points inside the learned normal-region boundary and a negative value for points outside it, mirroring the same sign convention already covered for Isolation Forest's decision_function output.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: One-Class SVM adapts the maximum margin idea from ordinary SVM to learn a boundary around normal data alone.
It is purpose-built for the realistic anomaly detection scenario of training on normal examples with no labeled anomalies at all.
It effectively finds the tightest region that still contains almost all the normal training data.
The RBF kernel, exactly as in ordinary SVM, lets the boundary capture curved, irregular shapes rather than just a simple linear region.
The nu parameter controls boundary tightness, trading off between flagging fewer or more points as anomalies.
Compared to Isolation Forest, it offers a more precise, explicit boundary at a higher computational cost on large datasets.
Feature scaling remains essential, since One-Class SVM inherits ordinary SVM's dependence on distance and kernel calculations.
It fits well when only normal training examples exist and the normal region has a genuinely complex, non-convex shape.
Next up: Local Outlier Factor, a density-based method that compares each point's local density to that of its neighbors.
